questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct preposition: The cat jumped __________ the wall and ran into the garden.
questions.explanation: 'Over' indicates movement from one side to the other of an obstacle (the wall). 'Above' is wrong — it means at a higher position without crossing; 'upon' is wrong — it means on top of and staying there; 'across' is wrong — it is used for flat surfaces, not vertical obstacles like walls.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements about the correct use of articles:

(i) 'She is __________ honest woman' requires the article 'an' because 'honest' starts with a silent 'h'.
(ii) 'He went to __________ university' requires the article 'a' because 'university' starts with a /juː/ sound.
(iii) 'I saw __________ one-eyed man' requires the article 'a' because 'one' starts with a /w/ sound.
(iv) 'She bought __________ European car' requires the article 'an' because 'European' starts with a vowel letter.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'An honest' is correct because 'h' is silent (i-correct); 'a university' is correct because the sound is consonant /juː/ (ii-correct); 'a one-eyed' is correct because 'one' starts with /w/ (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because 'European' starts with /juː/ (consonant sound), so it takes 'a', not 'an'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: Neither the teacher nor the students __________ present at the assembly yesterday.
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it — here 'students' (plural), requiring 'were'. Also, 'yesterday' demands past tense. 'Was' is wrong — the nearest subject 'students' is plural; 'is' is wrong — it's present tense; 'has been' is wrong — it's present perfect, not simple past.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The correct sentence is 'He has been living here since 2010' (not 'from 2010').
Reason (R): With the present perfect continuous tense, 'since' is used for a point in time, while 'from' is used with simple tenses.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Since 2010' is correct with present perfect continuous (A is correct). 'Since' pairs with perfect tenses for a point in time, while 'from' is used with future or simple tenses (R is correct and explains A). Option 2 is wrong because R directly explains the grammar rule; Option 3 is wrong because R is a valid rule; Option 4 is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct conjunction: He worked very hard __________ he could pass the examination.
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces a purpose clause — he worked hard with the aim of passing. 'Because' is wrong — it introduces reason, not purpose (it would mean the passing caused the hard work); 'although' is wrong — it introduces concession/contrast; 'unless' is wrong — it introduces a negative condition.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences have the blanks correctly filled?

(i) The furniture __________ (was) very expensive. [treating furniture as uncountable]
(ii) The news __________ (are) shocking. [treating news as plural]
(iii) Mathematics __________ (is) my favourite subject. [treating as singular]
(iv) The police __________ (have) arrested the criminal. [treating as plural]

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Furniture was' is correct — furniture is uncountable singular (i-correct); 'Mathematics is' is correct — subjects ending in -ics take singular verbs (iii-correct); 'The police have' is correct — police is a collective noun always treated as plural (iv-correct). Statement (ii) is wrong because 'news' always takes a singular verb ('The news IS shocking').

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: She is older __________ me by two years.
questions.explanation: 'Than' is used for comparisons (older than). 'Then' is wrong — it refers to time, not comparison; 'from' is wrong — 'older from' is not standard English; 'to' is wrong — 'senior to' is correct but 'older to' is not standard usage.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following blanks with the correct words:

Column I:
(a) He is __________ to his country. (faithful)
(b) She gave a __________ speech. (short and powerful)
(c) The task was __________. (very difficult)
(d) His behaviour was __________. (worthy of praise)

Column II:
(i) arduous
(ii) loyal
(iii) commendable
(iv) concise

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Loyal' means faithful to one's country (a-ii); 'concise' means short and powerful (b-iv); 'arduous' means very difficult (c-i); 'commendable' means worthy of praise (d-iii). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b); Option 3 swaps (c) and (d); Option 4 swaps (b) and (c).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: By the time we reached the station, the train __________.
questions.explanation: Past perfect 'had left' is used for an action completed before another past action ('reached'). 'Left' is wrong — simple past doesn't show the sequence clearly; 'has left' is wrong — present perfect cannot combine with past time reference; 'was leaving' is wrong — it implies ongoing action, not completion.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct article: __________ Ganga is the longest river in India.
questions.explanation: 'The' is used before names of rivers (the Ganga, the Nile, the Amazon). 'A' is wrong — indefinite articles are not used with specific proper nouns; 'An' is wrong — same reason plus wrong vowel-consonant match; 'No article' is wrong — river names require the definite article 'the'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'He insisted __________ going alone' is correctly filled with 'on'.
(ii) 'She is afraid __________ spiders' is correctly filled with 'of'.
(iii) 'I congratulated him __________ his success' is correctly filled with 'for'.
(iv) 'They blamed him __________ the accident' is correctly filled with 'for'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Insisted on' (i-correct); 'afraid of' (ii-correct); 'blamed for' (iv-correct). Statement (iii) is wrong because the correct collocation is 'congratulated him ON his success', not 'for'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: If I __________ a bird, I would fly to the mountains.
questions.explanation: 'Were' is used in the subjunctive mood for unreal/hypothetical present conditions (second conditional). 'Am' is wrong — it's indicative mood, not hypothetical; 'was' is wrong — formal grammar requires 'were' after 'if' in unreal conditions; 'had been' is wrong — that would make it a third conditional (past unreal).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct word: The principal __________ (accepted/excepted) all the applications except the incomplete ones.
questions.explanation: 'Accepted' means received/approved, which fits the context of applications. 'Excepted' is wrong — it means excluded (the sentence already uses 'except' for exclusion); 'expected' is wrong — it means anticipated, not received; 'exempted' is wrong — it means freed from an obligation.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns and 'many' is used with countable nouns.
Reason (R): Uncountable nouns cannot be counted individually, so they require quantifiers that indicate amount, not number.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: 'Much' goes with uncountable and 'many' with countable nouns (A is correct). Uncountable nouns need amount-based quantifiers because they can't be individually counted (R is correct and explains A). Option 2 is wrong because R explains the logic; Option 3 is wrong because R is correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Hardly had he reached home __________ it started raining.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly...when' is the correct correlative pair indicating something happening immediately after. 'Than' is wrong — 'hardly...than' is grammatically incorrect (though sometimes confused with 'scarcely...when' or 'no sooner...than'); 'then' is wrong — it's an adverb of time, not a conjunction here; 'before' is wrong — it reverses the time logic.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct modal verb: You __________ not park your vehicle here; it is a no-parking zone.
questions.explanation: 'Must not' expresses prohibition (you are forbidden to park here). 'Should not' is wrong — it merely advises against something, not prohibits; 'can not' is wrong — it expresses inability, not prohibition; 'would not' is wrong — it expresses willingness/refusal in conditional sense.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following blanks are correctly filled?

(i) She __________ (laid) the book on the table. [past tense of 'lay' = to place]
(ii) He __________ (lied) on the bed for an hour. [past tense of 'lie' = to recline]
(iii) The hen __________ (layed) an egg this morning. [past tense of 'lay' = to produce eggs]
(iv) She __________ (lay) awake all night. [past tense of 'lie' = to recline]

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Laid' is the correct past tense of 'lay' (to place) (i-correct); 'lay' is the correct past tense of 'lie' (to recline) (iv-correct). (ii) is wrong — the past tense of 'lie' (to recline) is 'lay', not 'lied' ('lied' is past of 'lie' meaning to tell an untruth); (iii) is wrong — 'layed' is not a word; the past tense of 'lay' (to produce eggs) is 'laid'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Each of the students __________ given a certificate.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' takes a singular verb because 'each' refers to individual members one at a time. 'Were' is wrong — plural verb doesn't agree with singular 'each'; 'are' is wrong — present tense and plural; 'have been' is wrong — plural auxiliary doesn't agree with 'each'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentences with the correct prepositions to fill the blanks:

Column I:
(a) She arrived __________ the airport on time.
(b) He has been waiting __________ two hours.
(c) The book is __________ the table.
(d) We went __________ a walk in the evening.

Column II:
(i) for
(ii) on
(iii) at
(iv) for

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Arrived at' the airport (a-iii); 'waiting for' two hours (b-i); book is 'on' the table (c-ii); went 'for' a walk (d-iv). Option 2 puts 'on' with airport incorrectly; Option 3 puts 'on' with waiting; Option 4 puts 'for' with arrived.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The committee __________ divided in their opinions on the matter.
questions.explanation: When 'committee' refers to individual members acting separately (divided opinions), it takes the plural verb 'were'. The pronoun 'their' also confirms plurality. 'Was' is wrong — the sentence emphasizes individual disagreement; 'is' is wrong — past context and plurality; 'has' is wrong — doesn't fit grammatically.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'He is good __________ mathematics' takes the preposition 'at'.
(ii) 'She is fond __________ chocolates' takes the preposition 'of'.
(iii) 'They are keen __________ learning' takes the preposition 'on'.
(iv) 'I am angry __________ you' takes the preposition 'on'.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Good at' (i-correct); 'fond of' (ii-correct); 'keen on' (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because the correct collocation is 'angry WITH you' (for a person), not 'angry on'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: No sooner did the bell ring __________ the students rushed out.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner...than' is the correct correlative structure. 'When' is wrong — 'when' pairs with 'hardly/scarcely', not 'no sooner'; 'then' is wrong — it's an adverb of sequence, not a conjunction; 'that' is wrong — it doesn't form a valid correlative with 'no sooner'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct pronoun: Between you and __________, this plan will not work.
questions.explanation: 'Me' is the object form used after the preposition 'between'. 'I' is wrong — it's the subject form and cannot follow a preposition; 'myself' is wrong — reflexive pronouns are only used when subject and object are the same person; 'mine' is wrong — it's a possessive pronoun, not an object pronoun.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'The scenery here are beautiful' is incorrect.
Reason (R): 'Scenery' is an uncountable noun and always takes a singular verb.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: The sentence is incorrect — it should be 'The scenery here IS beautiful' (A is correct). 'Scenery' is uncountable and needs a singular verb (R is correct and explains why 'are' is wrong). Option 2 is wrong because R directly explains A; Option 3 is wrong because R is correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: She __________ her keys somewhere in the house but cannot remember where.
questions.explanation: Present perfect 'has kept' indicates a past action with present relevance (she still can't find them). 'Had kept' is wrong — past perfect requires another past reference point; 'was keeping' is wrong — past continuous doesn't fit the meaning; 'is keeping' is wrong — present continuous implies ongoing deliberate action.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The teacher asked the students __________ they had completed their homework.
questions.explanation: 'Whether' introduces an indirect yes/no question (had they completed or not?). 'That' is wrong — it introduces statements, not questions; 'what' is wrong — it asks for specific information, not yes/no; 'which' is wrong — it asks for selection from options, not completion status.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following sentences correctly fill the blank with the appropriate word?

(i) The __________ (principal) of the school addressed the students.
(ii) Honesty is the best __________ (principle).
(iii) The __________ (effect) of the medicine was immediate.
(iv) The new law will __________ (affect) thousands of people.

Select the correct combination:
questions.explanation: 'Principal' = head of school (i-correct); 'principle' = a rule/belief (ii-correct); 'effect' = result/noun (iii-correct); 'affect' = to influence/verb (iv-correct). All four use the correct homophones in their proper context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Despite __________ hard, he could not pass the exam.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a gerund (verb + ing) or noun phrase. 'To work' is wrong — infinitives don't follow 'despite'; 'worked' is wrong — past tense forms don't follow 'despite'; 'work' is wrong — base form doesn't follow 'despite' (though 'despite hard work' as noun would be fine).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following sentences with the correct words to fill the blanks:

Column I:
(a) I am looking __________ my lost wallet.
(b) Please look __________ this matter urgently.
(c) She looks __________ to her grandmother.
(d) He looked __________ the word in the dictionary.

Column II:
(i) into
(ii) for
(iii) up
(iv) up

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Looking for' = searching (a-ii); 'look into' = investigate (b-i); 'looks up to' = admires (c-iv); 'looked up' = searched in reference (d-iii). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b); Option 3 wrongly assigns 'up' to investigating; Option 4 wrongly assigns 'up' to searching.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Either the manager or his assistants __________ going to handle this project.
questions.explanation: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearest subject — 'assistants' (plural), so 'are' is correct. 'Is' is wrong — 'assistants' is plural; 'was' is wrong — context requires present tense; 'has been' is wrong — singular and present perfect doesn't match.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'I have been to Delhi twice' correctly uses present perfect with 'been'.
(ii) 'He has gone to Delhi' means he is still in Delhi.
(iii) 'She has been to London' means she visited London and has returned.
(iv) 'They have gone to the market' means they have returned from the market.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: 'Have been to' indicates past visit with return (i-correct, iii-correct); 'has gone to' indicates the person is still there (ii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong because 'have gone to the market' means they are still at the market, not that they have returned.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: She is __________ intelligent that she can solve any problem quickly.
questions.explanation: 'So...that' is the correct correlative structure (degree + result). 'Very' is wrong — 'very' is not followed by 'that' clause; 'too' is wrong — 'too...that' is grammatically incorrect (use 'too...to'); 'much' is wrong — 'much intelligent that' is not valid grammar.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank with the correct word: The government has taken several __________ (steps/measures) to control inflation.
questions.explanation: 'Measures' means actions/steps taken for a purpose. 'Measurements' is wrong — it refers to the size/amount of something measured; 'measuring' is wrong — it's a gerund/present participle; 'measurable' is wrong — it's an adjective meaning able to be measured.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Given below are two statements, one labeled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The sentence 'I look forward to hear from you' is grammatically incorrect.
Reason (R): 'Look forward to' is a phrasal verb where 'to' is a preposition (not part of infinitive), so it must be followed by a gerund (-ing form).

Choose the correct option:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.correctAnswer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation: The correct form is 'look forward to hearing' (A is correct — 'hear' should be 'hearing'). The 'to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition requiring a gerund (R is correct and explains A). Option 2 is wrong because R directly explains the error; Option 3 is wrong because R is correct; Option 4 is wrong because A is correct.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The mother along with her children __________ going to the temple.
questions.explanation: When a subject is followed by 'along with', the verb agrees with the main subject only — here 'mother' (singular), requiring 'is'. 'Are' is wrong — the phrase 'along with her children' does not make the subject plural; 'were' is wrong — past tense not required; 'have been' is wrong — present perfect continuous doesn't fit the context.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: She is too tired __________ any more work tonight.
questions.explanation: 'Too + adjective + to + infinitive' is the correct structure. 'Doing' is wrong — gerund cannot follow 'too...'; 'for doing' is wrong — this structure doesn't apply with 'too'; 'to doing' is wrong — after 'too + adjective', the infinitive (to + base form) is required.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: I wish I __________ taller.
questions.explanation: 'Were' is used in the subjunctive mood after 'wish' for present unreal situations. 'Am' is wrong — it's indicative, not subjunctive; 'was' is wrong — formal grammar requires 'were' after 'wish' for hypothetical present; 'would be' is wrong — 'would' is not used after 'wish' for present states.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'The train leaves at 6 PM tomorrow' correctly uses simple present for scheduled future events.
(ii) 'I am meeting him tomorrow' correctly uses present continuous for planned future arrangements.
(iii) 'I will go to the market yesterday' is correct usage of simple future.
(iv) 'She is going to start a new job next month' correctly uses 'going to' for planned future actions.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Simple present for timetables/schedules (i-correct); present continuous for personal arrangements (ii-correct); 'going to' for plans/intentions (iv-correct). Statement (iii) is wrong because 'will' (future) cannot be used with 'yesterday' (past) — it's a contradiction.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Not only __________ he rude, but he was also dishonest.
questions.explanation: 'Was' matches the past tense established by 'was also dishonest' in the second clause. 'Is' is wrong — it's present tense conflicting with 'was' in the second part; 'had' is wrong — 'had he rude' is grammatically invalid; 'has' is wrong — present tense conflict.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following blanks with the correct determiners:

Column I:
(a) __________ milk is left in the bottle. (small amount)
(b) He ate __________ apples. (more than two)
(c) __________ student must submit the form. (all without exception)
(d) There are __________ books on the shelf. (not many)

Column II:
(i) Every
(ii) A little
(iii) Few
(iv) Several

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'A little' = small amount of uncountable (a-ii); 'several' = more than two (b-iv); 'every' = all without exception (c-i); 'few' = not many (d-iii). Option 2 assigns 'few' to milk (uncountable error); Option 3 mismatches determiners; Option 4 swaps 'every' and 'few'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The old man walks slowly __________ he has arthritis in his knees.
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for walking slowly. 'Although' is wrong — it introduces contrast, not reason; 'unless' is wrong — it introduces a negative condition; 'so that' is wrong — it introduces purpose, not reason.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: She asked me where I __________.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, when the reporting verb is past ('asked'), the tense shifts back — present becomes past: 'live' → 'lived'. 'Live' is wrong — tense should shift in reported speech; 'am living' is wrong — present continuous without backshift; 'do live' is wrong — emphatic present without backshift.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Which of the following correctly fill the blanks?

(i) He is __________ (elder/older) than his brother.
(ii) My __________ (elder/older) sister is a doctor.
(iii) She is the __________ (eldest/oldest) member of the team.
(iv) He is __________ (elder/older) to me by five years.

Select the correct combination of correct sentences:
questions.explanation: 'Elder sister' is correct — 'elder' is used as an adjective before a noun for family members (ii-correct); 'elder to' is correct — 'elder' takes 'to' not 'than' (iv-correct). (i) is wrong — 'elder' is not followed by 'than' (use 'older than'); (iii) is wrong in the given context — 'oldest' is correct for non-family comparisons among a group (team), 'eldest' is for family.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The patient had been suffering __________ fever for a week before he visited the doctor.
questions.explanation: 'Suffer from' is the correct collocation for diseases/illnesses. 'By' is wrong — 'suffer by' is not standard; 'with' is wrong — though sometimes used informally, 'suffer from' is the correct formal usage for diseases; 'of' is wrong — 'suffer of' is not grammatically valid.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Consider the following statements:

(i) 'A ten-year-old boy' uses a hyphenated compound adjective correctly.
(ii) 'The well known author' should be hyphenated as 'well-known' before a noun.
(iii) 'She is twenty one years old' needs a hyphen: 'twenty-one'.
(iv) 'A four story building' does not need any hyphen.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Compound adjectives before nouns are hyphenated: 'ten-year-old' (i-correct); 'well-known' before a noun (ii-correct); numbers twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated (iii-correct). Statement (iv) is wrong — 'four-story' should be hyphenated as a compound adjective before 'building'.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The manager insisted that every employee __________ present at the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Be' is the subjunctive form required after verbs of insistence/demand/suggestion (insist that + subject + base verb). 'Is' is wrong — indicative present doesn't follow 'insist that'; 'was' is wrong — past indicative is not the subjunctive form; 'will be' is wrong — modal 'will' is not used in subjunctive mandative clauses.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: He is one of those students who __________ always punctual.
questions.explanation: In 'one of those...who', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'students' (plural), so the verb is 'are'. 'Is' is wrong — 'who' refers to 'students', not 'one'; 'was' is wrong — past tense doesn't match the present context; 'has been' is wrong — singular verb for a plural antecedent.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText:
Match the following idioms with the words that complete them:

Column I:
(a) To burn the midnight __________
(b) To let the cat out of the __________
(c) A blessing in __________
(d) To hit the nail on the __________

Column II:
(i) head
(ii) disguise
(iii) bag
(iv) oil

Choose the correct match:
questions.explanation: 'Burn the midnight oil' = study/work late (a-iv); 'let the cat out of the bag' = reveal a secret (b-iii); 'a blessing in disguise' = something good from bad (c-ii); 'hit the nail on the head' = say exactly right (d-i). Option 2 swaps (a) and (b); Option 3 swaps (b) and (c); Option 4 swaps (c) and (d).

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: The number of accidents on this road __________ increased significantly this year.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' is always followed by a singular verb (the number = a single quantity). 'Have' is wrong — 'the number' is singular; 'are' is wrong — singular subject needs singular verb; 'were' is wrong — past tense and plural don't fit.

questions.subject: A
questions.questionText: Fill in the blank: Had I known about the meeting, I __________ attended it.
questions.explanation: 'Would have + past participle' completes the third conditional (past unreal condition with 'had known'). 'Will have' is wrong — future perfect doesn't pair with past perfect condition; 'should' is wrong — it needs 'have attended' and changes the meaning; 'could' is wrong — it needs 'have attended' to form a valid conditional.
